strengths: Well-motivated empirical analysis identifying two overlooked factors (token diversity and cross-modal 'information migration') via clear preliminary studies (Figures 1-2), providing intuitive justification for the proposed two-stage design.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 benchmarks (8 image, 4 video) and two model scales (7B/13B), with consistent, sizeable improvements over strong recent baselines (FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2) at multiple compression ratios.
Practical, training-free and architecture-agnostic design that is compatible with efficient attention operators (e.g., FlashAttention), making it easy to adopt without retraining.
Detailed ablation studies (Stage 1 vs Stage 2 contributions, threshold τ, layer selection strategy) that support design choices and demonstrate complementary benefits of the two stages.

Rich qualitative analysis (Appendix E) comparing attention-driven vs diversity-driven token retention and free-form long-response QA, illustrating tangible benefits of the proposed method beyond aggregate benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix B assumes visual and text embeddings occupy strictly orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), which is not an established or empirically verified property of LVLM embedding spaces (visual and text tokens are jointly attended to and interact throughout the network); the 'proof' of orthogonality between redundancy measures is essentially a restatement of this assumption rather than a genuine structural insight, limiting its scientific value.

DivPrune, a directly relevant diversity-based pruning baseline cited in related work, is not included in the empirical comparison, leaving open how ToDRE's diversity mechanism compares against the most similar prior approach.

All experiments are conducted on a single model family (LLaVA-NeXT 7B/13B); demonstrating generalization to other LVLM architectures (e.g., Qwen-VL, InternVL) would substantially strengthen claims of broad applicability.

The measured efficiency gains over the closest competitors (FasterVLM, GlobalCom2) are quite small in FLOPs and throughput (Table 3), with most benefit coming from prefilling-stage token reduction already achieved by other one-stage methods; the added complexity of the second stage yields only marginal additional efficiency.

The method introduces several additional hyperparameters (retention count k, threshold τ, candidate layer set) whose sensitivity is only explored on the 7B model in the appendix; it is unclear whether the reported default settings transfer well across models/tasks without retuning.

The explanation for why ToDRE sometimes exceeds the uncompressed baseline's performance on video benchmarks (claimed reduction of 'interference from redundant tokens') is asserted rather than rigorously validated, leaving this interesting but potentially confounded result under-explored.

strengths: The paper identifies two underexplored and reasonably well-motivated criteria for visual token pruning—intra-modal diversity and cross-modal task relevance—complementing the commonly used attention-based importance criterion. The motivating example (Figure 1) and empirical analysis (Figure 2, 'information migration') provide a clear rationale for the two-stage design.

The proposed method is training-free, architecture-agnostic, and simple to implement (greedy k-center selection + attention-ratio-based layer pruning), making it easy to adopt and compatible with efficient attention operators such as FlashAttention.

Extensive experiments across 12 benchmarks (8 image, 4 video) and two model scales (7B/13B) consistently show ToDRE outperforming several strong recent baselines (FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2) at multiple compression ratios, including under extreme 90% pruning.

Thorough ablations are provided, including the individual contribution of each stage, threshold sensitivity for layer selection, and choice of candidate layers, which support the design decisions and improve reproducibility.

Efficiency metrics (FLOPs, memory, throughput) are reported alongside accuracy, giving a fairly complete picture of the speed-performance trade-off, and qualitative case studies (Figures 6-7) help illustrate the intuitive benefit of diversity-driven retention over attention-driven pruning.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix B for 'orthogonality' of intra- and cross-modal redundancy relies on a strong and largely unverified assumption (W_V^T W_T = 0) that visual and textual embeddings occupy strictly orthogonal subspaces within a shared LLM embedding space; this assumption is not empirically validated and is unlikely to hold exactly in real trained models, so the theoretical result provides limited practical insight beyond restating the intuition already given in Section 3.2.

The core techniques (greedy k-center diversity sampling, cross-modal attention ratio thresholding) are conceptually simple extensions/combinations of existing ideas (k-center clustering, VTW's information migration observation, [CLS]-attention pivot selection from FasterVLM); the novelty is more in careful engineering and combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic insight, and the paper could better discuss overlap with the concurrent/prior DivPrune approach that also uses diversity-based pruning.

The efficiency gains from Stage 2 (relevance-driven full token removal) appear marginal for standard benchmarks with short answers (Table 4), and the paper explicitly acknowledges this, meaning the practical benefit of the second stage is mostly hypothetical for realistic short-answer VQA/benchmark settings and only anecdotally demonstrated for long-form generation (single case study, no quantitative long-generation latency/accuracy table).

Some hyperparameters (threshold τ=0.03, candidate layers at L/2, 5L/8, 6L/8, 7L/8) appear tuned specifically for LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B and Vicuna-based decoders; it is unclear how sensitive these choices are when transferred to substantially different LLM backbones or decoder depths, which could limit out-of-the-box generalizability despite the training-free claim.

The main comparison table excludes some baselines (FastV, SparseVLM) from the 13B setting due to reported transferability issues, and GlobalCom2 is excluded from video benchmarks; while explained, this makes some comparisons less complete.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated two-stage framework that separates intra-modal (diversity) redundancy from cross-modal (relevance) redundancy, addressing a real limitation (positional/attention bias) of prior attention-based pruning methods.

Extensive empirical validation across 4 LVLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B) and 12 benchmarks (8 image, 4 video), consistently outperforming strong baselines (FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2, DivPrune) at multiple retention ratios (25%, 10%).
Thorough ablation studies (pivot selection strategy, threshold τ, layer selection for Stage 2) and efficiency analysis (FLOPs, memory, throughput) that substantiate design choices.
Training-free, plug-and-play, and architecture-agnostic method that is straightforward to adopt without retraining, which increases practical impact.

Good qualitative analysis (attention-map visualizations, long free-form video captioning case study) that helps illustrate why the method preserves more informative tokens than attention-based pruning.

The appendix includes an attempt at theoretical justification (orthogonality of intra- and cross-modal redundancy) and additional analysis of decoding-stage attention, which strengthens the motivation for the two-stage design.
weaknesses: The core techniques (greedy max-sum diversification for token selection, layer-wise pruning based on attention decay) are incremental over existing works (DivPrune's max-sum diversity formulation, VTW's information migration concept); the novelty is more in combining these two ideas than in a fundamentally new mechanism.

The theoretical 'orthogonality' proof in the appendix is a fairly trivial probabilistic identity under an assumed strict orthogonality of visual/textual subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), which is not verified empirically and does not hold exactly in practice for learned embeddings sharing a space; the practical relevance of this proof to justifying the two-stage design is weak and somewhat window-dressing.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (DivPrune) are often modest (e.g., 95.0% vs 93.5% at 10% retention, or smaller margins in Table 1/2/3), and some benchmarks show ToDRE underperforming compared to baselines (e.g., VizWiz in Table 1 13B, MLVU in Table 2 at 10%), suggesting the gains, while consistent, are not uniformly large.

Efficiency gains from Stage 2 (relevance-driven layer pruning) are shown to be marginal for most benchmarks because typical VQA-style outputs are short, and the claimed benefit for long-form generation is only illustrated qualitatively (one case study) rather than quantitatively benchmarked on tasks with long outputs.

The layer selection strategy (fixed fractional depth of 7L/8) and threshold τ appear to be manually tuned constants validated only on LLaVA-NeXT-7B; it's unclear how well these hyperparameters transfer across the other backbones (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL2) without additional tuning, which could affect claimed plug-and-play generality.

Pivot token selection relies on a [CLS] token that not all vision encoders have (e.g., possibly SigLIP-based encoders in Qwen2.5-VL), and while a random-selection fallback is mentioned, its performance on non-CLS backbones is not explicitly validated in the main results.

Some experiments are run on a single RTX 3090, and reported efficiency numbers (throughput, memory) may not generalize to other hardware or batch sizes; reproducibility could benefit from more implementation details (code availability is not explicitly confirmed in the excerpt).
